parsed_answer.content: Reactor Core is the foundational library for reactive programming on the JVM, implementing the Reactive Streams specification to handle asynchronous, non-blocking data streams. At its heart, the library provides two primary publishers: Mono and Flux. A Mono represents a reactive stream that emits at most one item—either a single value or an empty completion signal—making it the ideal abstraction for operations like database lookups by ID, HTTP GET requests, or single-value calculations. Conversely, a Flux is a reactive stream capable of emitting zero to N items, followed by a completion or error signal. It is the workhorse for processing collections, event streams, or paginated data sets. Both types are lazy by nature; they do not execute until a subscriber invokes the subscribe() method, triggering the assembly-time pipeline to materialize into a runtime execution graph.

items: Backpressure handling: Both types implement the Subscriber/Subscription protocol, allowing the consumer to signal how much data it can process, preventing memory overflow in producers.

Assembly vs. Execution: The pipeline definition (e.g., .map(), .flatMap()) is purely declarative. The actual execution occurs on the thread pool defined by the Scheduler, which is decoupled from the definition phase.
Error Propagation: Errors are terminal signals in both Mono and Flux. Once an error occurs, the stream is terminated, and the error signal propagates downstream to the subscriber's onError handler.

parsed_answer.content: A common production pitfall is 'blocking the event loop.' Because Reactor operators are non-blocking, calling a synchronous, blocking I/O operation (like legacy JDBC or Thread.sleep()) inside a map() or flatMap() will starve the underlying Scheduler threads. Always offload blocking calls to a dedicated Schedulers.boundedElastic() thread pool to prevent the entire reactive pipeline from grinding to a halt.
